stem: Which three parts define a web origin under the same-origin policy?
options: IP address, port and cookie name
explanation: RFC 6454 defines an origin as scheme, host and port. `https://shop.example` and `https://shop.example:8443` are different origins.
optionNotes: Correct: change any one of them and it is a different origin.
The path and query do not count.
Cookies are not part of an origin, and the host is a name, not only an IP.
The user agent has nothing to do with origins.

stem: A cookie holds `dXNlcj1ib2I7cm9sZT11c2Vy`. A tester decodes it to `user=bob;role=user` without any key. What does this show?
options: It is strongly encrypted with a server-side key
It is only Base64-encoded, which hides nothing
It is a salted password hash stored by the site
It is signed, so the server would reject any change
explanation: Encoding is not encryption. A role stored in a client-side value must be protected by a server-side session or a verified signature.
optionNotes: Encryption would need a key to reverse.
Correct: encoding is reversible by anyone.
A hash cannot be reversed to readable text.
Nothing here proves a signature; an unsigned role value invites tampering.

stem: Which category is A01 in the OWASP Top 10:2025?
explanation: Broken Access Control is A01 in both the 2021 and 2025 lists; in 2025 it also absorbs SSRF.
optionNotes: Security Misconfiguration moved up to A02.
Injection is A05 in 2025.
Correct: it keeps first place from 2021.
Cryptographic Failures is A04 in 2025.

stem: A logged-in user visits a forum page that silently submits a hidden form to their bank's transfer URL. The bank sees a valid session cookie but an `Origin` header from the forum. What attack is this?
explanation: CSRF abuses the browser's habit of attaching cookies. An anti-CSRF token, SameSite cookies and an Origin check stop it.
optionNotes: Fixation plants a known session ID before login.
No script runs on the bank's own pages.
SSRF makes the server, not the browser, send the request.
Correct: a forged cross-site request rides the victim's cookies.

stem: Which Burp Suite tool lets a tester resend a single captured request by hand, change it and compare the responses?
explanation: Repeater is the manual tool; Intruder is the automated one. The exam likes that split.
optionNotes: Intruder automates many requests from payload lists.
Correct: manual, one request at a time.
Sequencer measures the randomness of tokens.
Collaborator detects out-of-band interactions.

stem: What is the difference between spidering and forced browsing?
options: Spidering needs valid credentials; forced browsing sends no requests
Spidering guesses unlinked paths; forced browsing follows the links shown
Both only read robots.txt and sitemap.xml to list the site's pages
Spidering follows links the app shows; forced browsing guesses unlinked paths
explanation: Crawlers such as ZAP Spider map linked content. Tools such as gobuster and ffuf find content nobody links to, which shows up as bursts of 404s.
optionNotes: Neither statement is true.
This reverses the two terms.
robots.txt is one input, not the whole technique.
Correct.

stem: Which risk is API1 in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)?
explanation: BOLA is the most common API flaw: the API does not check that the caller may access the object whose ID it received.
optionNotes: That is API7.
That is API2.
Correct.
That is API9.

stem: Your service receives payment events by webhook. How do you confirm that a delivery really came from the provider?
options: Recompute the HMAC of the raw body with the shared secret and compare it
Check that the request arrived over HTTPS with a valid certificate
Check that the User-Agent header names the payment provider
Reply 200 at once and trust the event type in the JSON payload
explanation: GitHub signs deliveries with HMAC-SHA256 in `X-Hub-Signature-256`; Stripe signs a timestamp plus the body. Compare in constant time.
optionNotes: Correct: only a holder of the secret can produce a valid signature.
TLS protects the channel but does not identify the sender.
Any client can set any User-Agent.
Trusting the payload is exactly what forged deliveries exploit.

stem: A penetration test report says an XSS bug could let an attacker copy the session cookie through `document.cookie`. Which attribute on that cookie closes this particular path?
explanation: HttpOnly limits the damage of XSS by keeping the session cookie out of `document.cookie`. It does not stop XSS itself.
optionNotes: Path limits which URLs receive the cookie.
Secure only limits the cookie to HTTPS.
SameSite controls cross-site sending, not script access.
Correct.

stem: A code review finds user input concatenated into a database query. The team proposes adding a WAF rule. What is the best fix?
options: Hide the database error messages from users on every page
Rely on the WAF rule alone, since it blocks the known patterns
Use parameterized statements; keep the WAF rule only as a stopgap
Move the database to a separate server behind a firewall
explanation: OWASP's primary injection defense is parameterized APIs. A WAF rule is defense in depth or virtual patching until the code is fixed.
optionNotes: Hiding errors only makes the flaw harder to see.
A WAF blocks known patterns but leaves the flaw in the code.
Correct: parameterization removes the flaw; the rule is virtual patching.
Moving the database changes nothing about the query.
